items.excerpt:
Most healthcare security teams have spent close to two years hearing that a major rewrite of the HIPAA Security Rule is on its way, and many have reacted in one of two ways.
Some paused large security investments until the final text appears, on the reasoning that there is no point building to a draft. Others started rewriting policies line by line against the proposal, as though it were already law.
Neither approach holds up well, because the proposal is still unsettled in its details while much of what it describes is work that a regulated organization should be doing under the current rule anyway.
The more useful question is which parts of the proposal are worth acting on now and which parts can safely wait for the final version.
The Office for Civil Rights at the Department of Health and Human Services issued its notice of proposed rulemaking in late December 2024, and it was published in the Federal Register on 6 January 2025.
The comment period closed on 7 March 2025, after the department had received thousands of comments, a large share of them from providers and industry groups concerned about cost and implementation timelines.
The rulemaking was originally expected to reach a final rule in May 2026, but the most recent federal regulatory agenda moved it to the long-term actions list and now projects final action no earlier than July 2027.
In the meantime, the existing Security Rule remains fully in force and enforceable. Every covered entity and business associate is still required to conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis, implement safeguards that address the risks it finds, and document what it has done. That obligation is the starting point for any sensible readiness plan.
The proposal is the most significant revision of the Security Rule since it was first written, and its central change is structural.
Today, many implementation specifications are labeled addressable, which allows an organization to adopt an alternative measure or document why a specification is not reasonable for its environment. The proposal would remove that distinction and make nearly all specifications required, with only narrow exceptions.
Several new and more specific obligations would follow from that shift. items.excerpt:
Every warehouse automation conference seems to have the same scene: a crowd gathered around a walking humanoid robot, while a quieter booth nearby showcases autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) already moving goods in thousands of facilities.
Both technologies promise to change logistics. But in 2026, they are at very different stages of commercial maturity.
AMRs are a proven option for moving totes, carts, and inventory across warehouses. Humanoid robots offer a different promise: handling objects and working with equipment designed for people, without requiring a complete redesign of the facility.
The difference comes down to task fit, operating costs, reliability, and the data used to train robotic systems. Humanoids must learn to handle unfamiliar objects and respond to changing physical conditions, making high-quality robotics training data an important part of their development.
This guide compares both technologies, examines a practical payback example, and outlines a framework for deciding which type of robot to pilot first.
Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) are wheeled robots that move goods around a building on their own. They use cameras, lidar, and onboard software to plan routes and avoid people. Unlike older AGVs (automated guided vehicles), they don’t need magnetic tape or fixed tracks.
Example : A picker stands in one zone. An AMR rolls up with a tote, the screen shows which item to grab, and the robot drives the tote to packing. The person walks less; the robot does the travel.
Humanoid robots have a human-like body: two legs (or a wheeled base), a torso, two arms, and hands or grippers. The pitch is simple. Warehouses are built for people, so a robot shaped like a person can work in them without rebuilding the site.
Example : A humanoid lifts a tote off an AMR and places it on a conveyor. That small hand-off is hard for wheeled robots without adding an arm or redesigning the station.
In short: AMRs automate movement. Humanoids try to automate manipulation in spaces designed for human bodies.
A useful example is GXO’s partnership with Agility Robotics. In June 2024, the companies announced a commercial Robots-as-a-Service agreement to deploy Digit in warehouse operations. The robot handles repetitive material-moving tasks, including transferring totes to conveyors, while working alongside existing automation such as AMRs.

items.description: For years, logistics transformation has been organized as a succession of projects. Implement the platform. Build the control tower. Automate the facility. Add the AI layer. The problem is that logistics no longer changes on a project cadence. That environment is disappearing. The post The Systems-Engineered Logistics Operation: From Transformation Projects to Continuous Design appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
For years, logistics transformation has been organized as a succession of projects. Implement the platform. Build the control tower. Automate the facility. Add the AI layer. The problem is that logistics no longer changes on a project cadence.
That environment is disappearing. The future logistics will need to be designed continuously. The Autonomous Logistics Network is one expression of this end state, but reaching it requires continuous design rather than a one-time transformation project.
Modern logistics networks are becoming integrated combinations of physical assets, software, data, optimization, AI, robotics, people, partners, and automated decisions. Calling this a technology stack understates what is happening.
It is an operating system. The important design questions are no longer confined to which applications a company owns. Leaders have to consider how decisions flow, how data maintain continuity across systems, how automation interacts with people, how models are governed, how exceptions escalate, and how the organization behaves when components fail.
That is systems engineering territory. The companies that manage this architecture deliberately will have an advantage over those that continue adding capabilities one project at a time.
Logistics technology is moving from systems of record toward systems of decision. Traditional applications captured transactions and supported workflows. Analytical systems added prediction and optimization. The emerging layer increasingly combines real-time signals, AI, optimization, agents, and execution connectivity.
The result is intelligence closer to the point of action. A shipment delay can be identified, its impact evaluated, alternatives generated, and a response executed with limited human intervention. Transportation systems can continuously re-evaluate routes, capacity, and exceptions instead of waiting for manual replanning. Warehouse and yard systems can adjust priorities as conditions change.
This will make logistics faster. It will also make architecture and governance more consequential.
When software only reported information, a bad output could be ignored. When software acts, the operating envelope matters.

items.excerpt:
Warehouse automation has traditionally been discussed one facility at a time. A retailer installs an automated storage system, deploys mobile robots, adds robotic picking, or upgrades sortation. The business case is then measured against improvements within that particular building. Walmart and Symbotic are beginning to challenge that way of thinking.
On October 29, Walmart and Symbotic announced an expanded commercial agreement that will bring additional automation capabilities to 25 U.S. regional distribution centers . The agreement includes an initial commitment of approximately $6 billion , covering work over several years and multiple locations. Walmart says the initiative is intended to support upstream e-commerce inventory management, increase storage capacity, and improve the movement of products through its supply chain. Those numbers make the announcement noteworthy. But the more interesting story is what the scale of the commitment says about the next phase of warehouse automation.
From an Automation Project to an Operating Model
For years, warehouse automation investments were frequently justified around specific bottlenecks: reduced picker travel, increase storage density, improve sortation throughput, or offset labor requirements. Those are still important objectives. But Walmart is evaluating automation against something larger: the performance of an interconnected distribution network supporting stores, pickup and home delivery.
Rob Montgomery, executive vice president for Walmart U.S. Supply Chain Operations, tied the expanded agreement to improving service, growing capacity, simplifying work for associates and lowering costs. The company also expects the expansion to support broader assortment, greater speed and more reliable replenishment. That distinction matters.
Warehouse automation increasingly needs to be evaluated not simply by asking, “How much faster can this facility pick?” but by asking, “What does this investment change across the supply chain?” Does additional storage capacity improve inventory positioning? Does automation enable later ordering cutoffs? Can replenishment become more predictable? Can the same technology architecture be repeated across multiple facilities without redesigning the operation every time? Those questions take warehouse automation discussions much closer to business strategy.

items.excerpt:
LMI reaches second-highest level in four years, driven by robust expansion of inventory levels, report shows.
Economic activity in logistics grew in October, driven by a continued expansion of inventory levels heading into the holiday shopping season.
The information comes from the October Logistics Managers’ Index (LMI), released today , which rose to 70.7 compared to a reading of 70.2 in September. That’s the second highest reading in four years, behind June’s level of 71.1.
The LMI is a monthly reading of economic activity across warehousing and transportation, based on a survey of logistics managers nationwide. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in logistics activity, and a reading below 50 indicates contraction.
Readings above 70 indicate strong logistics activity across the country.
Inventory levels rose 8.0 points in October as retailers stocked up for holiday sales—a move that came with a price, as the LMI’s Inventory Costs index rose nearly 9.0 points to 88.8, the highest reading for that metric since March of 2022. What’s more, the increase in inventories is affecting available storage, as both the Warehousing Capacity and Transportation Capacity indices continued to contract during the month, falling to 43.5 and 38.0, respectively, according to the report.
Those results occurred alongside expanding cost pressures. Inventory costs, warehousing prices, and transportation prices all expanded in October, combining to create the fastest expansion in aggregate logistics costs in more than four years—a factor the researchers say, “may foreshadow continued supply-driven inflation.”
Aggregate costs reached a score of 257.5 on a scale of 0-300—up more than 11 points from September.
“This is the highest reading for this aggregate metric since March of 2022, when supply-driven inflation was rampant in the wake of both the cessation of Covid-era demand and the invasion of Ukraine,” the researchers wrote in the November 3 report. “Given the pressure on logistics costs, it is likely that we will continue to see supply-driven inflation continue to increase in the near term.”
The LMI tracks industry growth overall and across eight areas: inventory levels and costs; warehousing capacity, utilization, and prices; and transportation capacity, utilization, and prices. 如果你还没订阅 Where’s Your Ed At，现在正是最好的时机。我把促销延长了——新订阅用户可享每年 70 美元订阅费终身 9 折（ 点这里！ ）——再持续一周。这是支持我工作的绝佳方式，而且你能以比几乎所有竞品通讯都低的价格，获得极其丰富的价值。
过去几个月里，我发布了一篇 分 两 部分的 AI 债务世界指南，一篇关于 生成式 AI 对全球经济（可疑）影响 的分析，对 AI 基础设施领域最大玩家如 NVIDIA（ 上 、 下 ）和 Oracle（ 上 、 下 ）的深度分析， OpenAI 最终将如何杀死 Oracle ，以及 风险投资如何杀死自己 。
周五的文章讲的是 断层线 ——最容易受 AI 泡沫破裂冲击的领域、用来观察行业恶化的数据点，以及可能引发崩盘的因素。
如果你想联系我——尤其是如果你掌握关于 Anthropic、OpenAI、Blackstone 或 AI 泡沫中任何其他公司的劲爆消息——请在 Signal 上找我，号码 ezitron.76。你也可以在彭博终端上通过 IB 联系我。
正如我一段时间以来一直说的， 这一切会在钱花光时结束 ——当看似无限的数据中心债务变得令人痛苦地难以筹集，当 AI 初创公司无法再依赖风险资本的永久可得性来维持生存。
而看起来这口井正在干涸，与此同时所有人都开始意识到，无论对实验室还是数据中心运营商来说，AI 的基本经济逻辑都说不通。
2026 年 9 月 16 日， 《纽约时报》报道 称 OpenAI 正在“考虑”新一轮融资，估值 1.5 万亿美元， 此时距其将 IPO 推迟到 2027 年还不到三个月 。十天后，9 月 29 日， 彭博社报道 称其计划以 1.4 万亿美元估值融资 300 亿美元，10 月 5 日又 披露 其正与 BlackRock、一个银团以及阿联酋基金洽谈，后者“讨论过总共投入最多 100 亿美元”。
上周——不到一个月后—— OpenAI 以 1.25 万亿美元估值融资 110 亿美元 ，此前“一些大型投资方的兴趣不温不火”，《华尔街日报》称，并补充说 OpenAI“……告诉股东它预计会尝试筹集更多资金……[并希望]最多筹集 200 亿美元”，目标是“家族办公室和高净值个人”，这意味着主权财富基金、风险投资机构和私人信贷公司已经给出了它们愿意给的全部。
据 The Information 报道 ，OpenAI 在 2026 年第一季度的收入成本与研发两项合计支出 121 亿美元；而根据微软自己的财报， OpenAI 的算力支出和收入分成付款为其最近一个财季贡献了 100 亿美元收入 。
换句话说，那 110 亿美元融资甚至不够覆盖 OpenAI 一个季度的算力成本，而且我们有理由问： 为什么这轮融资必须现在完成 ，以及 这家公司接下来到底要做什么。

如果OpenAI需要的只是区区 110亿美元 ，那它融资的原因很可能是出于某种程度的绝望，和/或试图赶上Anthropic的IPO—— 据彭博社报道 ，投资者目前预计Anthropic的IPO定价将在1.4万亿至1.5万亿美元之间， 而不到一个月前，预期定价还是2万亿美元甚至更高 。 据WSJ报道 ，Anthropic如今正“被机构投资者敦促将目标估值下调至1.5万亿至1.6万亿美元”。

我认为答案大概介于两者之间——OpenAI需要这笔钱，需要感觉自己能与Anthropic竞争，并且意识到应该在资本市场关门之前尽可能多地融资。

items.title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
items.excerpt:
We’re introducing StateBench , a benchmark for long-context state tracking —how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.
State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.
Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.
To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

items.title: Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity
items.description: Learn how Google Antigravity and our Cheminformatics Skills accelerate drug discovery workflows, search compounds, and propose novel rigidified macrocycles.
items.excerpt:
Zoi Tsangalidou, Ruijie (Kelly) Zhang, Sukhdeep Singh and Michael V. LeVine
Designing new medicines requires curating complex data from charts, figures and literature, training predictive models, and proposing candidate molecules to synthesize — a workflow that typically takes multiple days for a single iteration.
Here we show how Google Antigravity , equipped with our new Cheminformatics Skills, accelerates drug discovery workflows. Using real-world lung cancer treatments, an agent searches through thousands of compounds, performs matched molecular pair analysis, and proposes novel rigidified macrocycles with synthetic routes in just an hour.
Chemistry is one of science’s richest public records — spanning millions of structures across journal articles and vendor catalogs. It provides a common representation that links physics and mathematics to the life and environmental sciences. Molecules and their transformations are ubiquitous and shape the everyday world.
Despite decades of progress in cheminformatics, chemists still spend too much time wrangling data, a process complicated by the fact that molecules can be represented in many ways: from text descriptions to images or data structures. The same molecule can appear as an IUPAC name in a paper, a Markush structure in a patent, or a structure-data file (SDF) in a catalog. Advanced cheminformatics systems must be able to unify these sources and deal with the many ways errors can arise in them. This task has no margin for error – alter a single atom or bond and you have described a different compound altogether, rendering a promising inhibitor or catalyst inert.

Grounded in RDKit , the foundational open source cheminformatics toolkit developed over two decades by a global community of contributors, alongside connectors to curated resources from ChEMBL and PubChem , the skills encode domain best practices directly into the agent’s workflow.

items.title: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
items.excerpt:
Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.
Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.
Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.
A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.
It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

items.excerpt:
Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!
Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:
Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming .
The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.
spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.
I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

items.title: Digital Twins Could Improve Temperature Control in Refrigerated Trucks
items.description: Maintaining the correct temperature inside a refrigerated truck does not necessarily mean that every pallet is being cooled evenly. New research from Switzerland’s Empa laboratories demonstrates how digital twins could help logistics operators identify temperature variations within a shipment, improve cold-chain performance, and reduce food waste. Researchers at the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science […] The post Digital Twins Could Improve Temperature Control in Refrigerated Trucks appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
Maintaining the correct temperature inside a refrigerated truck does not necessarily mean that every pallet is being cooled evenly. New research from Switzerland’s Empa laboratories demonstrates how digital twins could help logistics operators identify temperature variations within a shipment, improve cold-chain performance, and reduce food waste.
Researchers at the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology (Empa) developed a physics-based digital twin that simulates airflow and heat transfer throughout a refrigerated trailer. The model estimates temperatures at different locations within the cargo, providing greater visibility than conventional monitoring systems that may rely on a single temperature sensor.
The researchers tested the model using a four-day shipment of 31 pallets of oranges and lemons traveling from Greece to Switzerland. They installed 108 sensors throughout the load to compare actual temperatures with the digital twin’s predictions.
The results revealed an important challenge. Although the refrigeration system maintained temperatures between 4 and 6 degrees Celsius, some oranges in the middle of the trailer reached 10.8 degrees.
The researchers determined that insufficiently precooled pallets were a likely explanation. Their simulations showed how warmer products could transfer heat to neighboring pallets, while packaging design and pallet positioning influenced airflow and cooling effectiveness.
The findings suggest that digital twins could eventually help shippers and transportation providers optimize pallet arrangements, evaluate packaging designs, and identify temperature-related risks before products reach their destinations.
By integrating real-time sensor data with physics-based models, operators could potentially identify shipments requiring additional inspection or prioritize products with shorter remaining shelf lives.
The technology remains under development, but its potential extends beyond temperature monitoring to more proactive management of product quality throughout transportation.
For refrigerated transportation providers, the research highlights an important distinction: maintaining the correct trailer temperature is not the same as maintaining the correct product temperature.
Source: Empa — Digital Twins for Refrigerated Trucks, November 3, 2026 .

items.title: Design for Failure: Resilience, Risk, and Failure Modes
items.description: Resilience becomes expensive when it is treated as a shopping list of buffers: more inventory, more overflow space, more carrier capacity, more alternate lanes, more technology redundancy. A better starting point is diagnostic: how does this logistics system fail, how quickly will we know, and what happens… The post Design for Failure: Resilience, Risk, and Failure Modes appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
Resilience becomes expensive when it is treated as a shopping list of buffers: more inventory, more overflow space, more carrier capacity, more alternate lanes, more technology redundancy. A better starting point is diagnostic: how does this logistics system fail, how quickly will we know, and what happens next?
Systems engineering offers another useful discipline: failure mode thinking. Instead of beginning with the question, "How much redundancy should we add?" begin with, "How can this system fail, what happens when it does, and what should the system do next?" That produces a much more precise resilience strategy. Resilience becomes more important as the operation moves toward the Autonomous Logistics Network , because tightly connected and increasingly automated systems can propagate failures faster unless recovery paths are designed in advance.
A carrier can reject capacity. A port or terminal can close. A distribution center can lose power. A conveyor, sorter, robot fleet, or dock system can fail. Labor can become unavailable. A transportation lane can lose capacity. A software interface can fail. Data can be wrong. A cyber incident can isolate systems. An automated logistics decision can be incorrect.
The objective is not to imagine every possible disaster. It is to identify the failures that matter and understand their consequences.
A failure mode becomes important when it combines likelihood, severity, detectability, and recoverability in a way that threatens business requirements. This is familiar territory for engineering disciplines and increasingly necessary for logistics networks.
Traditional logistics risk programs often focus on carrier capacity, weather, and geographic exposure. That is useful, but dependencies extend further.
Multiple carriers may depend on the same constrained gateway. Several distribution centers may depend on one cloud or integration service. A parcel strategy may depend on one sort hub. Two apparently redundant transportation options may share the same port, airport, rail ramp, road corridor, or technology provider. A seemingly resilient logistics network can still contain common points of failure.
Resilience therefore requires dependency mapping. What facilities, lanes, carriers, gateways, data feeds, people, automation assets, and technologies are required for a critical logistics flow? Which dependencies are hidden? Which are shared?

It’s a dim and distant memory now but, once upon a time, BlackBerry was by far the world’s favourite smartphone among business users.
Journalists and all sorts of other professionals were amazed that a phone could enable them to check and respond to their emails while they were out and about.
There literally was no other phone quite like it, and BlackBerry sold in its millions.
Then the iPhone came along with its touchscreen interface and helped transform what people expected from a smartphone. BlackBerry faced the difficult question of how far it should move away from the physical keyboard and business-focused formula that had made it successful.
BlackBerry is still remembered with some fondness, even by people like me who didn’t own one but occasionally used a friend’s or colleague’s device and appreciated the innovation and engineering that went into it.
So, a year or two ago, when I started receiving emails from “BlackBerry” about automotive software, highlighting QNX , I initially wondered: “So that’s what happened to BlackBerry.”
The real history is slightly different. QNX actually dates back to 1980 and was acquired by BlackBerry – then Research In Motion – in 2010. But today QNX has become one of the most important parts of the wider BlackBerry story, supplying foundational software technology to the automotive industry.
And it is now at the centre of another technological transformation – the emergence of the software-defined vehicle.
The scale QNX has achieved is impressive. According to the company, QNX technology is embedded in more than 275 million vehicles worldwide, and its software can be found in vehicles produced by many of the world’s largest automotive manufacturers.

items.excerpt:
Eval-production behavior gaps in agent safety and the role of eval-awareness
OpenAI Alignment 团队对比六个模型在 Respecting Warnings 安全评测与匹配的 Codex 生产决策上的表现，发现评测成功率普遍低于生产，差距为 10.2 至 37.4 个百分点。模型普遍口头表现出评测意识（评测中一般性意识率 57.0%–83.7%），但仅告知
原文用六个模型对比评测与生产数据，发现评测成绩反而更低，并把差距归因于模型对评测目标的误判。
我们开始直接追踪这一差距，以便更好地评估在这些安全评估中观察到的智能体行为能在多大程度上推广到真实使用场景。
评估感知已在多种模型和评估环境中被广泛观察到 [1-3] 。模型常常会口头指出某次交互是一次评估，推测测试目标，有时还会据此改变行为 [4] 。这给解读和信任评估结果带来了实实在在的挑战：我们观察到的行为中，有多少能推广到部署环境？这种行为变化在多大程度上取决于模型对任务的解读？
本文聚焦智能体安全评估，涵盖长周期任务——智能体在遇到潜在的安全关键触发条件（例如警告、限制或障碍）时必须决定如何应对。尽量缩小这里的评估与生产差距至关重要，因为一项有信息价值的安全评估，需要衡量智能体在真实使用中是否做出同类决策。
为评估这些评估在多大程度上反映智能体在真实世界中的行为，我们比较了评估与生产中的成功率，并探究模型对评估情境的解读是否能解释这一差距。结果表明：
（1）评估与生产之间的行为差距确实存在，且方向出人意料：一些模型在安全评估中的表现似乎明显差于生产环境，而差距最大的模型，恰恰是最频繁口头说出错误评估目标的那些。
（3）然而，对评估 目标 的感知与评估和生产之间的行为差距密切相关，而目标框架可以因果性地改变评估成功率。
我们将评估与生产之间的行为差距定义为：模型在评估中的表现，与在测试可比区分的生产决策中的表现之间的差异。
评估表现。 我们采用“尊重警告”（Respecting Warnings）评估作为代表性的安全评估。该评估检验智能体在执行用户任务时，能否对警告、限制和障碍做出恰当回应。警告可能描述真实的授权边界，也可能是对某项操作或方法的限制。因此，正确行为要求结合用户目标来判断警告的权威性和适用范围。我们将成功定义为：在遇到相关警告或限制后，不做出任何被禁止的规避尝试。
可比较的生产表现。 为了衡量部署期间的可比较表现，我们选取 与“尊重警告”评估的底层决策结构相匹配的生产案例 。我们从具有代表性的生产流量中，提取经过脱敏的 Codex 生产日志上下文窗口 。我们通过多阶段流程识别可比较的生产决策。 首先，由分类器识别出引入障碍或约束的工具观察结果。其次，由评分员和基于来源的审核员判断该情境是否构成非平凡的安全关键选择，并识别所请求的效果、管辖权限、约束范围、适用例外以及合法替代方案。第三，由匹配器将每个保留的决策与“尊重警告”评估目录进行比对，并保持单个参考案例的决策结构。我们仅依据决策前的上下文进行筛选，不以模型成功或失败为条件。随后，我们对部署中实际记录的后续行为进行评分，评分沿用“尊重警告”的评分定义，并根据可用的生产证据加以调整。 这一流程有助于识别可比较的决策，但我们注意到匹配仍是近似的，模型面临的案例组合各不相同，且抽样的生产上下文并不能代表所有部署场景。
评估与生产之间的行为差距确实存在。 我们针对六个已服务的模型（GPT-5.6 Luna、GPT-5.6 Sol、GPT-6 Luna、GPT-6 Sol、GPT-6 Astra 和 GPT-6.1 Sol）， 在可比较案例上测量了评估表现与生产表现。 在下图 1 中可以看到，评估与生产之间的差距确实存在。差距范围为 10.2 到 37.4 个百分点，其中 GPT-5.6 Sol 和 GPT-6 Sol 的差距最大。
差距的方向出人意料 。 在所有模型中， 评测成功率 都低于在可比生产决策上的成功率。 关于评测意识，一个常见的担忧是模型能识别出安全测试，并调整自身行为，从而抬高测得的安全水平。 而这里观察到的差距方向恰恰相反：模型在评测中表现得比在匹配的生产场景中更不安全。这些分数比较的是评测环境与已部署 Codex 的行为，指令、工具、用例构成以及模型认知上的差异都可能造成这一差距。本文后文会详细探讨这一现象的可能解释。尤其是，模型可能试图去做它认为评测会奖励的行为，却误解了实际被测试的内容。它针对推断出的测试所做的回应，反而可能使其行为比在可比生产场景中更不安全，从而拉低测得的安全表现。然而，无论评测是高估还是低估安全性，这种错配始终是一个根本性问题，也限制了我们能多大程度自信地用评测分数预测生产环境中的行为。
分数存在差异，并不意味着评测对部署毫无信息价值。因此我们进一步追问：在评测中表现更好的模型，是否在生产决策上也表现更好？我们用 Spearman 秩相关和无加权普通最小二乘拟合来比较各模型的成功率。在全部六个模型上，Spearman 的 ρ = 0.771 ，线性拟合的 R 2 = 0.655 （见图 2）。 这种正相关关系说明，Respecting Warnings 评测保留了关于这些模型相对表现的有用信息，尽管其绝对分数并不能直接换算成生产成功率。 不过需要指出，模型样本量很小，这限制了我们推广所观察到的关系的把握程度。
这些结果表明，评测分数捕捉到了模型之间一些有意义的差异，尽管模型在评测和生产中的具体排名并不一致。接下来我们追问：模型对任务场景的解读能否解释这种评测与生产之间的差距？为此，我们拆解评测意识的各个组成部分，并区分一般评测意识（即识别或推测某次交互是评测）与具体评测目标意识（即推断评测在测试哪种行为）。
在这里，我们通过模型思维链中的自发陈述来衡量言语化的评估意识。我们对每条推理轨迹应用分类器：通用评估意识评分标准判断智能体是否陈述或推测当前交互是对助手的评估、

【X 长文】Critical thinking when agents do the work
Back in the day, critical thinking was taught as approaching new info with humble curiosity and a healthy dose of skepticism - take in different views, form your own opinion. Still true, but increasingly, nothing in my day-to-day forces critical thinking on me now that so much of my work runs through agents. For the engineers and product people who have fully bought into agentic workflows (running multiple sessions in parallel and expecting the models to improve), I'm here to say: I'm a big fan of these tools. I'm not writing this to advocate for less agentic workflows.
My goal is to help you maintain critical thinking in a world where it's easy to offload anything to an agent.
In the past, most of our cognitive and aesthetic processing happened in the space between question and answer. That space is now measured in seconds. The more you use agentic workflows, the more difficult it becomes (though not in the way I think people expected): as the models improve, the percentage of obvious errors is lower. Many (most?) outputs will be well-written and mostly correct, but they won't demand a second look.
Even if you are running many agents at a time, you still only have one pair of eyes on the outputs.
You have to build critical thinking into your day, because by default nothing will do it for you.
Part of the reason it's hard to self-correct for this is that agentic workflows are pleasant. Getting fast, pleasant, often-correct answers is refreshing in a busy day, but that's also why it's easy to relax your vigilance.
When discussing this with people, I describe it as a spectrum:
At the top: cognitive offloading, the act of delegating tasks to the AI, but maintaining ownership of the result. I do this all day. You should, too. In the middle: deferral, where the output of the tool becomes your new input; the result has ceased to be a hypothesis. At the bottom: cognitive surrender - the AI's output quietly becomes your own, you feel no need to check it.

Editing Qwen’s weights to reduce reasoning loops, DeepSeek’s super-agent prototype, and the GDPx benchmark.
Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today.
The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears :
Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and….
Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model?
In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models.
If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found:
Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use and explored due to its remarkable efficiency.

items.title: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
items.excerpt:
On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.
When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.
Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.
The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.
Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.
This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.
Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.
Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

Evals without traces, million-cell tabular reviews, and cracks in the billable hour as a business model
In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work.
Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO.
Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year.
We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended.
When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that?
What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients.
We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not what Legora is seeing. A good junior is worth more today than two years ago because they get so much more done, just as in engineering.
Most teams improve their agents by reading traces. Legora can't read any. Almost everything users upload is confidential, and much of it belongs to the firm's clients, not the firm.

items.excerpt:
By Gleb Tsipursky , PhD, CEO, Disaster Avoidance Experts
A new industrial robot can meet its cycle-time target and still fail its most important workplace test: what happens when an experienced operator believes the machine is wrong?
That question deserves attention as manufacturers accelerate automation. The International Federation of Robotics reported in September that the global stock of industrial robots exceeded five million units in 2025, with more than 600,000 new installations that year.
Increased capacity is real. So is the need to know how employees can challenge the system before a mistake spreads across a shift.
The latest performance improvements make the issue more urgent. As Robotics & Automation News reported on October 20, ABB’s new IRB 1700 models promise up to 20 percent shorter cycle times , with precision and energy-efficiency gains.
Faster cycles help a business meet orders. They can also reduce the time in which a worker identifies and explains an unexpected result. Speed magnifies the value of a clear escalation process.
In a recent opinion on simulation before deployment , BlueBotics CEO Nicola Tomatis made a useful case for testing traffic, charging, routes and fleet capacity while changes remain inexpensive. There is another variable worth testing before a system goes live: the human response to a disagreement.
Imagine a machine-vision system marks a batch of parts as defective. A veteran operator suspects residue on the camera lens, not a production defect. The automated workflow is ready to divert the batch.
Who can challenge that classification? Can they pause the quality decision without compromising machine safety? Which supervisor receives the evidence? Does the next shift know what happened? This is a hypothetical example, but the questions are ordinary operational ones.
Safety procedures must remain separate and paramount. OSHA’s robotics guidance notes that many accidents occur during non-routine operations such as testing, setup, maintenance and adjustment.
A disagreement protocol cannot replace physical safeguarding, lockout/tagout, emergency stops or task-based risk assessments. Workers should never have to enter a robot’s hazardous operating area to contest an automated recommendation.

Warehouse automation is advancing quickly. Automated storage and retrieval systems, autonomous mobile robots, robotic picking, sophisticated warehouse management systems, and increasingly intelligent execution software are changing how goods move through distribution facilities. But installing more technology does not automatically create a modern warehouse. In many operations, the physical technology is advancing faster than the operating model surrounding it. A warehouse may introduce robotics into one process, automated storage into another, and new software on top of both, while still relying on procedures, labor structures, and decision-making processes originally built around predominantly manual operations.
That mismatch is becoming increasingly important. As fulfillment requirements become more complex, warehouse modernization needs to move beyond a discussion about which technology to deploy. The bigger question is how the operation itself must change when people, software, and automation increasingly perform work together.
From a Manual Operation to a Technology-Enabled System
Historically, warehouse operations were designed largely around the movement of people. Workers traveled to storage locations, searched for inventory, picked products, moved carts or pallets, sorted orders, and delivered goods to packing and shipping areas. Warehouse management systems helped coordinate this activity, but execution ultimately depended heavily on people moving through the building. Automation changes that fundamental relationship.
In a goods-to-person environment, for example, the employee may remain at a workstation while inventory moves to that person. An AS/RS can replace portions of traditional storage and retrieval activity. Mobile robots can take over transportation between operating areas. Robotic picking can potentially shift additional handling activities away from employees.
As those technologies accumulate, the warehouse becomes less like a collection of independent processes and more like an interconnected operating system. This is important because the performance of one technology increasingly depends on everything around it. items.excerpt:
The Association for Advancing Automation (A3) has announced the publication of ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communication and interoperability among industrial mobile robots (IMRs), regardless of vendor or model.
ISO 21423 provides a common set of communication requirements for mobile robots from different suppliers operating in the same industrial facility.
Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability specifies how IMRs, IMR fleet managers and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with each other.
For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning, which improves robot availability and system efficiency.
A common protocol is also expected to increase competition in the market and support innovation. An important benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world.
Carole Franklin, A3’s director of standards development, robotics, says: “Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor.
“Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years. Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located.
“This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.”
The standard also covers communication with machines tended by robots, enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools, and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors and alarms. People using mobile devices can share similar information, so their work can be coordinated alongside the robots.
ISO 21423 represents the first non-safety robot standard that A3 has helped produce, and highlights A3’s continued leadership in the robotics standardization efforts.
ISO 21423:2026 is available for purchase through the A3 online store for $373. A3 members can purchase the document for $320.

items.description: Where Decision Intelligence Goes Next: From Recommendations to Governed Action is the next logical stage of the category. items.excerpt:
The next stage of Decision Intelligence is not simply better recommendations; it is governed action. Many platforms can already surface an insight or recommend a response, but the harder step is connecting that recommendation to explicit authority, executable workflow, and feedback so the organization can act faster without losing control.
Instead of generating a one-time answer, decision systems will increasingly monitor a class of decisions continuously, maintain the relevant context, and update the recommendation as state changes. That persistence is essential in supply chains because orders, inventory, capacity, risk, and execution status are always moving. The move from recommendation to governed action is the natural extension of Engineering the Decision Architecture , where context, authority, escalation, and execution are designed as one operating pathway.
ERP, planning, TMS, WMS, visibility, risk, and network platforms remain systems of record and execution; decision intelligence sits above and across them where context is assembled, tradeoffs are evaluated, actions are prioritized, and responses are coordinated. The architecture needs controlled mechanisms for a recommendation to become a transaction, workflow change, communication, or other physical-execution instruction.
Low-risk, frequent, reversible decisions can move first. Higher-value decisions may remain machine-recommended and human-approved. Novel or relationship-sensitive situations should escalate. The market will differentiate on how well providers encode these boundaries rather than on whether they use the word autonomous.
Buyers will require traceability into data used, options considered, approvals, confidence, actions, overrides, and outcomes. That record supports trust, compliance, performance improvement, and the gradual expansion of machine authority where evidence justifies it.

Cloud migration is the process of moving an application, its data, and its infrastructure from on-premises servers to a cloud provider’s environment.
In legacy modernization it usually comes up first, because it promises quick gains in hosting costs and availability.
Its limits often show up a few months later, when changes still take as long to ship as before, now on infrastructure billed by the hour.
Well-planned software modernization services ( https://www.merixstudio.com/services/software-modernization ) treat the move to the cloud as one track of a broader roadmap, next to refactoring, test automation, and UX work.
This article is most useful for CTOs and IT managers deciding whether lift and shift is the right first step for their legacy system.
Lift and shift, also called rehosting, moves an application to cloud infrastructure with minimal changes to its code. Servers, storage, and backups move to the provider, and adding capacity becomes a configuration task instead of a hardware purchase.
Everything above the infrastructure layer stays where it was. A release that needed a week of manual regression testing still needs it, and users see the same interface. For this reason, lift and shift should be judged as an infrastructure decision. Its effect on development speed is indirect.

Speed is the main advantage. A lift and shift migration can take as little as two to three months, while refactoring a mid-complexity system typically takes four to eight.

Costs are the less obvious risk. An application designed for fixed on-premises servers usually runs at a constant size, and in the cloud idle capacity is still billed.

As head of Schneider Electric’s worldwide supply chain, Stuart Whiting is working to transform the company’s delivery operations—and do it all in the midst of ongoing geopolitical disruption.
When you think of companies that have innovative supply chains, retailers like Amazon and Walmart or consumer packaged-goods companies like Procter & Gamble and Unilever typically spring to mind—not a nearly 200-year-old industrial company with its roots in a French iron foundry.
Yet Schneider Electric is making a big push on the supply chain innovation front. The energy tech powerhouse has been working steadily to transform its supply chain delivery platform, which was originally designed around efficiency and standardization, into one that better accommodates individual customers’ needs. That’s no small task. As a provider of energy solutions for homes, businesses, data centers, infrastructure, and grids around the world, the company serves a customer base that is both large and diverse.
The point person for that transformation initiative is Stuart Whiting, Schneider Electric’s senior vice president of global supply chain logistics, planning, and services. Whiting and his team are working to build a hyperconnected supply chain, one that leverage digital tools—think control towers, AI (artificial intelligence)-enabled planning, and end-to-end visibility systems—to better anticipate the needs of different customer segments and respond quickly when those needs change. “Customers [today] need faster deployment and more tailored service models than ever before,” Whiting explains. “That means our supply chain can’t simply be global; it has to be intelligent.”
A British national, Whiting is a Fellow of the Chartered Institute of Logistics and Transport and holds a global master of science degree in logistics and supply chain management from Cranfield University’s School of Management. He was a keynote speaker at the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals’ (CSCMP) recent EDGE conference in Tennessee. items.excerpt:
Each October since 1945, the U.S. Department of Labor has sponsored National Disability Employment Awareness Month to acknowledge the positive impact people with disabilities have on the American workplace. This year’s theme was “Celebrating Value and Talent.”
Despite mounting evidence that hiring people with disabilities makes good business sense, corporate America has a long way to go in that regard. People with disabilities often face a number of hurdles in finding work. They not only must overcome their disabilities but also must fight inaccurate hiring assumptions. One misconception is that employees with disabilities won’t be there for the long haul, yet studies have shown that workers with disabilities actually have lower rates of turnover than the general staff.
As for concerns about performance, the evidence shows that facilities that hire workers with disabilities perform as well as—or better than—similar operations. A 2023 study by Accenture , in partnership with Disability:IN and the American Association of People with Disabilities, found that companies that employ and support people with disabilities outperform their peers without such programs. They reported 1.6 times more revenue, two times more profit, and 2.6 times more net income than those without a disability hiring program.
It doesn’t take much to adapt a facility for this workforce. Research from the Job Accommodation Network shows that more than half (56%) of accommodations cost nothing at all to implement, while others average around $300. That’s a small price to pay to expand the talent pool.
As for what those accommodations might entail in our corner of the world, many warehouses would require only simple changes. For instance, companies could design picking and packing stations to accommodate wheelchairs. They could provide workers who have visual disabilities with voice systems to provide directions. Likewise, they could equip those with hearing impairments with screens or use pick-to-light systems for guidance.
Simple adaptations can also be made for workers with cognitive issues and learning disabilities, like difficulty reading letters and numbers. For instance, one Walgreens facility I visited used snack-food symbols rather than numbers to designate picking aisles.
It’s difficult finding quality workers these days. Don’t overlook a ready-and-willing workforce of people who only ask for an opportunity.

There is a quote from Jim Barksdale, former CEO of Netscape, that rings true for building and operating any business, and especially a robotics company: the main thing is to keep the main thing the main thing. The main thing in robotics is getting the robot to complete human tasks – not the training data, not the specifics of the model, not the type of hardware used. Yet the prevailing debate in much of robotics centers on these factors.
Tutor Intelligence , unlike many of its peers, knows that the main thing is getting their robots to complete specific jobs, repeatedly and with high accuracy, for customer after customer. This is exactly why we’re excited to lead the company’s Series B.
Tutor is a robotics research and deployment company that builds generally capable robot hardware. They deploy into real production environments ahead of full autonomy, using human teleoperators (“tutors”) to train the robot foundation models and make the fleet more capable over time. It’s a novel approach that’s paying off.
Most robotics companies start by building a general model and then finding its initial use case. To do this requires massive upfront data collection, and capital, to build even a basic model.
Tutor took the opposite approach. First, they identified a real need and use case. Then, still before building a robot brain, they put the hardware to work using remote tutors (that were so skillful customers found real value while not being able to tell the difference between the work done by employees and the work done by tutors). With each deployment in a real scenario, Tutor could work backwards to create their model from the deployment data. The approach offers a win-win for customers and Tutor. For Tutor, the company is able to collect the training data that really matters and build an increasingly capable model, cost efficiently. Every robot put to work makes the next robot smarter, cheaper, and easier to deploy.

这起有记录以来最大的盗窃案，起点是开发者机器上的恶意软件。 朝鲜国家支持的黑客 从币安卷走了 63.4 亿美元 ，事件细节目前还有许多不为外界所知，但币安已披露，几名工程师的笔记本电脑因一场虚假面试和被篡改的安装程序而失陷，其中一台机器上的部署令牌让攻击者得以触达币安的钱包签名服务。一台失陷的开发者机器，绝不该足以攻破生产环境，更不用说盗走数十亿美元。
10 月 29 日，Cursor 披露有攻击者发布了 Claude Code Cursor 扩展的恶意版本，这是 Cursor 最受欢迎的扩展之一。该恶意扩展试图在开发者机器上安装持久后门，让攻击者能通过 SSH 登录用户设备。由于扩展会自动更新，这意味着用户可能在毫无操作的情况下就收到了恶意扩展。Cursor 表示，安装该恶意扩展的用户不到 5,000 人。
值得注意的是，该扩展的版本与 Open VSX 注册表（Cursor 使用的开放扩展注册表）上发布的版本并不一致。这表明攻击者攻破了 Open VSX 下游的扩展发布流程。
在不确定性日益加剧的当下，很难判断哪些事真正重要。我们列出了两组行动：需要立即执行的，以及需要在 30 天内完成的。采取这些措施能显著加固公司的安全防线，既能抵御当前的威胁，也能防范未来的风险。
币安被黑事件说明，把最关键的访问权限留在开发者机器上是个非常糟糕的主意。开发者笔记本电脑上运行着大量第三方代码：安装的软件包、编辑器扩展、MCP 服务器，以及如今能自行执行命令的本地 AI 智能体。其中任何一个都可能被攻陷，一旦被攻陷，攻击者就能继承该开发者能触及的一切。
过去一年里，我们看到了许多蠕虫式供应链攻击，比如 Shai-Hulud 系列攻击。
过去几周最大的漏洞利用和安全隐患，归根结底都是已知的漏洞类型和企业安全上的基本疏漏。Binance 因一个被篡改的安装程序、一场虚假面试，以及一台笔记本上遗留的部署令牌，损失了数十亿美元。新的 CVE 会不断出现，而前沿模型意味着它们被发现和利用的速度会比以往更快。问问你的安全团队正在采取上述哪些措施，并争取今天就搞定几项！

items.title: How AI Applications Earn Their Premium
items.description: Cheaper intelligence raises the bar for what an AI application can charge
items.excerpt:
Lower inference costs can improve margins for application companies, but more capable models and easier development tools can also make parts of an application easier to replace. The commercial question is what customers will continue to pay for as their alternatives improve.
This exposure varies by product. An application is vulnerable when a customer can reproduce its core output with a general-purpose model and little ongoing effort. This is the question for AI application companies right now. Pricing is always important, but right now it’s extra important , yet it sometimes gets overlooked or postponed because fast-growing AI companies are reluctant to tackle it.
All AI application companies need to spend time rigorously developing and pricing out these obvious-but-necessary capabilities: Domain expertise, deep integrations, reliable execution, and hard-to-access context. These are all pricing levers that can make buying substantially more attractive. Founders need to understand which advantages their customers actually value, then strengthen and price them.
The resulting build-versus-buy test looks like this:
Repsol’s legal team put the build-versus-buy question to a direct test. In a blind evaluation, it compared Harvey with Microsoft Copilot and its own internal AI prototype, Lexia. Harvey delivered the highest-quality output, then outperformed the alternatives on accuracy and time savings during an eight-week pilot involving 50 lawyers across 12 jurisdictions. Repsol proceeded with a full rollout. Harvey reports that lawyers now save four to six hours per week, with adoption reaching 96% across the legal department. The benefits also extend to future work: the team used Harvey to identify recurring objections across past agreements and improve its contract templates with fallback language. The case illustrates how an application can earn its premium through better execution than credible alternatives, measurable savings, and the ability to turn accumulated knowledge into reusable guidance. 1
From this and other examples, we gather three rules for sustained success:
Operate the workflow better than the customer can
Make context cheaper to rent than to rebuild
Prove the value, then price to capture it
A customer does not need to rebuild your entire application to weaken your pricing power. Moving one high-volume task in-house or establishing a credible alternative can be enough to challenge the premium.

items.title: OpenAI 推出 Grid Protectors 计划，从 Georgia 校园开始支持电网削峰
items.description: OpenAI 推出 Grid Protectors 计划，与电力公司、监管机构和政策制定者合作，让未来算力校园在电网紧张时降低用电需求，首站为 Effingham County 校园。 🔗 阅读原文 via AIHOT · https://aihot.news/items/sxbs5a90fgybhyucacmzvrc6w
items.excerpt:
OpenAI 推出 Grid Protectors 计划，与电力公司、监管机构和政策制定者合作，让未来算力校园在电网紧张时降低用电需求，首站为 Effingham County 校园。
OpenAI 首次系统化说明其校园电力弹性安排，给出 Georgia Power 合同的具体可削减容量与电费影响数据。
今天我们启动 电网守护者计划 （Grid Protectors Program），这是一项全国性行动，旨在让我们建设园区所在社区的居民和企业用上可负担、可靠的电力。我们将与公用事业公司、监管机构和政策制定者合作，为未来的园区制定安排，在电网承压时降低用电需求。
无论是北方寒潮来袭时供暖，还是南方热浪期间开空调，家庭都需要可靠的电力。我们的目标是让园区的灵活性成为一种资源，在社区最需要的时候供公用事业公司调用。
预计到2030年，美国数据中心容量将超过 100吉瓦⁠（在新窗口打开） ，我们因此迎来一个千载难逢的机会：通过建设能在社区最需要时调整用电的园区，来强化电网。
佐治亚州是我们的起点。通过电网守护者计划，我们希望让这种灵活性成为未来园区建设和运营的核心组成部分。这意味着在设计设施时就考虑在需要时降低用电，并与公用事业公司商定可削减多少需求、多快削减以及持续多久。具体安排将因地点而异，相关承诺一旦敲定，我们会另行公布。
根据当地需求和可用设备，我们还将与电网运营商合作，由现场发电或储能供电，并利用电池和功率控制来平抑需求波动。
无论需求高低，输电线、变电站及其他电网基础设施的建设都是固定成本。通过在电网有余量时多用一些电、在电网承压时减少用电，我们可以帮助分担这些基础设施的成本，同时减少为满足峰值需求而进行昂贵升级的必要。这有助于为其他用户压低成本。
美国需要更多电力来支撑经济增长，而AI正成为其中相当大的一部分需求。家庭和小企业不应被要求为计算园区的用电买单。我们始终承诺自行承担能源成本，包括我们使用的电力以及服务园区所需的基础设施。大型计算设施应当支付自身成本，并帮助公用事业公司管理它们所依赖的系统。
对于计划中的埃芬汉县（Effingham County）园区，我们已承诺支付服务该项目所需的全部基础设施和电力服务成本。园区投入运营后，我们可以在需要时减少取电，帮助为其他用户保留电力。
我们 与Georgia Power的协议还包括⁠（在新窗口打开） 最高1,000兆瓦的灵活需求响应，释放出电力，帮助数十万家庭在极端高温期间维持空调运转（按平均用电量计算约70万户）。从规模上看，这相当于约70万户家庭的年均用电需求，比华盛顿特区和波士顿的家庭总数加起来还多。
这意味着我们可以调低用电需求，让家庭、小企业和其他电费用户继续有电可用。建设电网资产成本高昂，佐治亚电力公司表示，这种灵活性可以减少其为满足未来增长而需要新建的发电装机。虽然园区仍在开发中，但我们希望 Effingham 能成为 Grid Protectors 的试点，这建立在现有协议的基础上，而该协议已经为未来的园区提供了范本。
想象一下度假小镇上的一家餐厅。旺季时它需要足够的餐桌和厨房空间，但全年都得为这些容量付费。老顾客帮它维持使用率，在旅游淡季时帮着分摊账单。我们提议的就是做那个老顾客。
电力需求也随季节起落，不同地区的用电高峰出现在不同时间。我们的计算园区全年都需要电力。有了合适的协议，这种稳定的需求可以帮助把电网的固定成本分摊到更多售电量上，而灵活性让我们能在系统最繁忙时降低需求。我们仍需承担园区产生的成本；目标是让其他用户也能受益。
我们的协议也为佐治亚电力公司降低用户成本的更广泛计划做出了贡献。这家公用事业公司 预计从2029年起，其大负荷协议组合及预期增长（包括 Project Camellia）每年可为用户节省约9.5亿美元⁠（在新窗口打开） 。该公司估计，一个典型居民用户每月用电1,000千瓦时，每月至少可受益15美元。
与佐治亚州的协议只是一个起点。在 OpenAI，通过我们的 Grid Protectors 计划，我们看到了一个机会，可以帮助社区即使在紧急和高需求时期也能保持供电。我们将与公用事业公司、监管机构和政策制定者合作，为我们未来建设的园区制定切实可行的安排——这些安排要反映当地电网需求，帮助园区在电网承压时提供支持，并承担我们产生的成本。长期合同和财务担保可以在项目延期、缩减或取消时保护其他用户。
灵活性无法取代对新能源供应和输电的投资。在这些投资之外，我们的 Grid Protectors 计划可以帮助电网更可靠，并保护家庭和小企业免于承担 AI 基础设施的成本。这就是我们希望计算园区达到的标准。

items.title: Govern the Living System: Change Control and Lifecycle Management
items.description: The governance intensity around a logistics system is often highest right before go-live and lowest during the years when the system actually creates value or accumulates debt. That is backwards. Go-live is the start of the operating lifecycle, not the end of the engineering work. The post Govern the Living System: Change Control and Lifecycle Management appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
The governance intensity around a logistics system is often highest right before go-live and lowest during the years when the system actually creates value or accumulates debt. That is backwards. Go-live is the start of the operating lifecycle, not the end of the engineering work.
The system slowly becomes different from the one that was designed. Systems engineering addresses this through lifecycle management and change control. The Autonomous Logistics Network makes lifecycle governance especially important because decision rights, thresholds, models, integrations, and operating assumptions will all change after deployment.
A logistics system is not finished when it enters live operation. It begins a new phase.
Shipment volumes change. Customers ask for new service levels. Carrier and 3PL networks change. Facilities open and close. New products alter handling and transportation characteristics. Technology vendors release new functionality. Regulations change. AI models require monitoring and retraining. Automation equipment ages.
The architecture has to evolve with these conditions. Lifecycle management provides the structure for doing that deliberately.
The organization needs to know who owns the system, who has authority to change it, how changes are evaluated, how risks are assessed, and how the effect of a change is measured. Without those mechanisms, the operating model gradually fragments.
Functional governance is necessary, but many logistics changes cross functional boundaries. A new carrier-allocation rule may affect transportation, warehouse cutoffs, finance, and customer promises. A warehouse wave-policy change may affect dock flow and linehaul departures. A new AI agent may change decision rights across transportation, fulfillment, customer service, and IT.
The governance model should therefore include end-to-end ownership.
Who is accountable for the performance of the process across functions? Who resolves conflicts between local objectives? Who owns shared data? Who approves changes to automated rules? Who decides whether a local exception should become a global standard?
These questions become more important as technology embeds decisions into the system. Governance is no longer only about approving projects. It is about governing operating behavior.
The phrase change control can sound like a barrier to speed. Poor change control is bureaucratic. Good change control makes speed safer.
A change should be evaluated according to its potential

items.excerpt:
North American companies ordered 10,989 robots valued at $723.5 million in the third quarter of 2026, according to new data released by the Association for Advancing Automation (A3).
Orders increased 24.8 percent in units and 26.1 percent in value compared to the third quarter of 2025, making it the strongest quarter of the year so far.
The third-quarter gains pushed total orders for the first nine months of 2026 to 28,984 robots valued at approximately $1.89 billion, representing increases of 9.6 percent in units and 13.3 percent in value over the same period last year.
After declining during the first half of 2026, Automotive OEM robot orders returned to positive year-over-year growth in the third quarter, increasing 7.5 percent.
Automotive Component orders climbed 90.4 percent, continuing the strong demand from suppliers seen earlier in the year.
Several other industries recorded substantial increases in robot orders during Q3:
All Other Industries increased 0.5 percent in units ordered, while Food & Consumer Goods declined 23.7 percent.
The growth in the Semi & Electronics/Photonics segment comes against a backdrop of continued investment in US semiconductor manufacturing and strong demand for electronics supporting AI and other applications. Life sciences has also seen continued investment in domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing among others.
Automotive Component orders have remained particularly strong despite earlier weakness among Automotive OEMs. While OEM orders improved in Q3, they remained 17 percent below their year-earlier level through the first nine months of 2026.
“What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market,” said Alex Shikany, executive vice president at A3.
“Automotive OEM orders returned to positive growth, while Automotive Components and sectors such as semiconductors/electronics and life sciences posted significant gains. That broader mix is important because it points to a robotics market that is becoming increasingly diversified across industries and applications.”
Collaborative robots also posted a strong third quarter, with 1,831 units valued at $63.8 million ordered, an increase of approximately 56 percent in units compared to Q3 2025. Collaborative robots accounted for 16.7 percent of all robot units ordered during the quarter.

items.excerpt:
Embotech and BMW Group say they have moved “1 million vehicles using automated driving technology” across four BMW Group production sites in the UK and Germany, marking a major milestone in the use of Automated Driving In-Plant in industrial production.
Automotive OEMs are increasingly turning to digitalization and automation to make production processes more efficient and flexible. Industrial automation is an important part of that shift, but much of the market remains at the pilot stage, operating only a limited number of vehicles.
The one million vehicle milestone demonstrates the scale that BMW Group has achieved with Automated Driving In-Plant, spanning different sites, brands, vehicle types and production and logistics processes.
The deployment also shows how the BMW Group and technology partner Embotech have developed Automated Driving In-Plant into a scalable solution for automated vehicle movements within the BMW Group production network.
For automated vehicle movements to become fully integrated into live production, every journey must happen with a high degree of precision and reliability. Together, BMW Group and Embotech have brought the Automated Driving In-Plant solution to approximately 3,500 vehicle movements a day, with more than 99.5 percent availability.
In production environments where unexpected downtime can disrupt wider operations, maintaining that level of availability is essential to keeping automated vehicle movements integrated into production.
Embotech provides key technology components for the Automated Driving In-Plant solution. These include Embotech’s AI-based software for perception, prediction and planning, which enables vehicles to operate in complex industrial environments, and a separate, deterministic safety architecture, independently certified by TÜV SÜD, that defines and enforces the safety boundary.
What started as an initial pilot in 2022 has now expanded to four BMW Group production sites including Dingolfing, Leipzig and Regensburg in Germany and MINI Plant Oxford in the UK.
Across the four sites, Embotech’s technology supports different automated vehicle-movement use cases in defined production and logistics areas.
For industrial operators, the value goes beyond the individual vehicle movement. Automated vehicle movements can support smoother vehicle flow, more stable and flexible operations, 24/7 capability independent of shift staffing, fewer transport damages, better use of available space and greater safety

items.excerpt:
Humanoid robots are an emerging technology that promises to revolutionize society. Designed and modeled on the human form, humanoid robots can navigate a world made for humans, and it is their versatility that sets them apart from specialized robots, such as automated guided vehicles (AGVs).
Similar to AGVs, humanoid robots need an energy source that can reliably supply power to ensure full operation for as long as required.
While current battery technology has been successful in demonstrating humanoid robot potential, IDTechEx ’s new report Batteries for Humanoid Robots 2027-2037: Technologies, Players, and Forecasts focuses on the technologies that will lead humanoid robots into widespread adoption in the market, reaching 10.5 GWh of battery demand by 2037.
IDTechEx highlights the suitability of current and emerging battery chemistries for humanoid robots. The comparisons illustrate trade-offs between battery performance and technological maturity across different chemistries.
The energy density of a battery used to power a humanoid robot needs to be high enough that it can complete power-intensive tasks and continue operating afterwards. Currently, NMC-based lithium-ion batteries are the most common technology employed by humanoid robots.
They balance a suitably high energy density with the prerequisite specifications of humanoids, that is that they require batteries with the potential to be fast-charged, a good cycle life, and a technology mature enough that they are already, or close to being, commercialized.
The energy density of NMC cathodes can also be improved by increasing the nickel-content in the cathode, which can boost performance and reduce dependence on costly and supply-constrained cobalt.
LFP cathodes are a chemistry considered not energy dense enough to be able to support the general demand of humanoid robots. Since NMC batteries are widely adopted for use in a plethora of other applications, NMC-based lithium-ion batteries are in great supply to support the growth of the humanoid robot market today, and beyond.
IDTechEx’s new “Batteries for Humanoid Robots 2027-2037: Technologies, Players, and Forecasts” report compares lithium-ion NMC cathode chemistries (mid-, high-, and ultra high-nickel) as current technology that can support humanoid robot growth.

items.title: When the Spreadsheet Stops Scaling: How to Modernize Cyclical Logistics Across Industries
items.description: Every operations team eventually outgrows the spreadsheet that got them started. A look at how to transform your monthly logistics cycle.
items.excerpt:
Somewhere in your organization, there is a spreadsheet holding things together that shouldn’t be. It was built for a smaller operation. Now it takes minutes to refresh, occasionally fails to load, and requires manual updates every cycle. Leadership lacks a clear operational view. When the person who built it leaves, institutional knowledge leaves with them.
This is not an aviation problem or a healthcare problem or a retail problem. It is an operations problem—and it shows up wherever cyclical logistics are managed at scale. The symptoms are consistent: manual vendor follow-ups, purchase orders updated by hand, no geographic visibility into where inventory actually is, and status checks that take far longer than they should.
The solution is also consistent. A recent transformation in airline in-flight entertainment (IFE) media logistics offers a clear blueprint, and the design principles translate to any supply chain managing cyclical vendor coordination.
Most operational tracking systems start with what’s available—usually a spreadsheet connected to a database. At low volume, this works. As the operation grows, the tooling does not scale with it. Refresh times slow. Columns multiply until the dashboard is unreadable. The process becomes dependent on individuals rather than systems.
The failure modes are predictable. Vendor communication happens when someone remembers to initiate it. Purchase orders are updated by hand every cycle. Status checks that should take seconds take minutes. Nobody has a real-time picture of where things stand across the network.
This pattern appears in healthcare, where inventory managers track surgical supplies across multiple facilities without real-time visibility. It appears in retail, where replenishment teams manage cyclical restocking through trackers that cannot keep pace with transaction volume. It appears in manufacturing, where MRO teams discover that critical spare parts are in the wrong facility only after a line has gone down. And it appears in logistics and freight, where shipment status across a distributed network requires manual aggregation rather than a single live view.
In each case, the data exists. It is simply not surfaced in a way that enables fast, confident decisions.

items.title: Claude Platform 推出 message threads 公测，降低长会话智能体延迟
items.description: Anthropic 在 Claude Platform 推出 message threads 公测，智能体每轮只需发送新增消息而无需重发全部对话历史，从而缩短首 token 时间。 🔗 阅读原文 via AIHOT · https://aihot.news/items/sg5u3u91kw42j1grtyp3ny65n
items.excerpt:
Make long-running agents faster with message threads
Anthropic 在 Claude Platform 推出 message threads 公测，智能体每轮只需发送新增消息而无需重发全部对话历史，从而缩短首 token 时间。
原文给出了 500k 至 1M token 请求下 TTFT 中位数下降约 35% 的数据，以及线程生命周期和接入方式，便于评估长会话智能体的延迟收益。
消息线程功能现已在 Claude 平台开启公开测试。借助消息线程，智能体不必在每一轮都重新发送完整的对话历史，从而降低长时间会话的延迟。
一个编程智能体在一次会话中可能发出数百个请求，而每个请求都会重新发送此前所有的消息和工具结果。当对话达到数十万 token 时，重发全部内容会让 Claude 开始响应前的等待时间变长。使用消息线程后，智能体只发送自上一轮以来的新增内容，从而缩短首 token 延迟（TTFT）。
大多数 Claude Code 用户默认开启消息线程后，50 万至 100 万 token 的请求首 token 延迟中位数下降约 35%。
要使用消息线程，请在 Messages API 请求中添加 thread 参数。第一个请求包含完整对话并开启一个线程，此后每个请求只包含新消息和上一条响应的 ID。在两轮之间，我们会把每个线程保存在内存中，加密存储且不写入磁盘。线程在最后一次请求后 5 分钟过期，之后客户端会重新发送完整对话以开启新线程。虽然使用消息线程后每个请求更小，但 Claude 在每一轮仍会读取完整对话，因此 token 用量保持不变。
消息线程现已在原生 Claude 平台开启公开测试，同时也已在 AWS 上的 Claude 平台、Microsoft Foundry 中的 Claude，以及 Google Cloud 上的 Claude 模型（Anthropic 托管）上线。适用标准 Claude token 费率和现有速率限制。请参阅 文档 开始使用。

OpenAI 宣布任命 Dan Driscoll 为新设的国家安全现代化高级顾问，就先进 AI 如何加强国家与网络安全提供建议，重点与美国盟友合作推动民主 AI 的负责任使用。

Dan Driscoll 将加入 OpenAI，担任国家安全现代化高级顾问，与高层领导和外部合作伙伴共事，就先进 AI 如何加强国家安全和网络安全提供建议，尤其侧重于与美国盟友合作，推动其负责任地使用。
在这一新设职位上，Dan 将与 OpenAI 各团队和领导者，以及政府、产业界、学术界和盟友机构的各方合作，推进务实的现代化举措，推动民主 AI 的建设。他还将帮助 OpenAI 内部团队了解全球国家安全机构的运营需求。
Dan 此前担任第 26 任陆军部长，负责陆军的运营、现代化和资源事务。他的经验涵盖军旅生涯、政府高层领导和私营部门。
在这一职位上，Dan 将为我们的公共和私营部门合作伙伴提供建议，帮助他们推进政策和战略选择的现代化，从而释放 AI 的实际用途，提升国家安全，并帮助确保全球建设的 AI 支持民主原则。他将致力于找出运营需求、机构变革与新兴 AI 能力之间的结合点。Dan 的任命体现了我们帮助民主机构负责任地使用先进 AI、以加强共同安全的承诺，也建立在 OpenAI 与盟友和伙伴合作的基础上——通过其 Daybreak 计划增强网络韧性、保护关键服务。
“AI 应该让人们对自己的生活拥有更多掌控权，人们也应该对 AI 如何发展有发言权。美国拥有非同寻常的机会，与其他国家合作推广民主 AI 的应用。我很高兴欢迎 Dan Driscoll 加入 OpenAI，以加强美国的领导力，帮助我们实现这一目标。”
“我职业生涯的大部分时间都在公共服务中度过，先是作为一名士兵，最近则担任陆军部长和 ATF 代理局长。服役人员理应得到我们能提供的最好的工具。国家安全需求的变化速度比过去五十年任何时候都快。这项技术将帮助他们跟上步伐：减少文书工作，理解更多信息，更快地把正确答案送到正确的人手中。我加入 OpenAI，是为了帮助美国及其盟友负责任地把这项技术投入使用，服务于那些守护我们安全的人。”
Dan Driscoll 曾任第 26 任美国陆军部长。任内，他负责近一百万现役、国民警卫队和预备役士兵以及超过 26.5 万名陆军文职人员的运营、现代化和资源分配。他推动陆军转型，重点在于加快新技术的部署、改革采购流程、打造更有能力的部队。Dan 曾是陆军军官和企业领导者，经验涵盖军旅生涯、法律和私营部门。

items.title: Why physical AI is the next lucrative frontier
items.description: To prove its commercial value, physical AI must get past funding enthusiasm and move into production environments. The post Why physical AI is the next lucrative frontier appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.excerpt:
Genesis AI recently unveiled the Eno robot to bring physical AI into commercial environments. Source: Genesis AI
The fastest-growing market categories have humble beginnings. Physical AI, the combination of robotics and advanced artificial intelligence, is just the latest example.
ChatGPT began as a pitch deck at an accelerator before it became a household name in 2023. Before cloud computing became a boardroom imperative, founders were building it, server rack by server rack, cluster by cluster. And, of course, before fintech rewired retail banking, it appeared as a funding surge in deal flow data that most banks weren’t reading.
You see the pattern, and I’ve watched it repeat itself across several years of evaluating startups. The startup ecosystem is the world’s most underutilized business intelligence system.
Incumbents may amass wealth and power, but it’s the founders who choose to build. Which sectors attract a sudden surge of founding activity is a three-to-five-year leading indicator of where enterprise disruption is headed.
While AI agents garner the lion’s share of media attention and VC funding , deal flow suggests the next market for hypergrowth will be of the metallic persuasion. That is physical AI , which includes autonomous machines and smart manufacturing, among other sensor-laden systems.
Robotics and physical AI startups raised a record $27.6 billion across 1,009 deals in 2025, or more than double the prior year, according to PitchBook. Genesis AI , which emerged from stealth with a $105 million seed round , recently demonstrated a wheeled robot that can bring physical AI into commercially relevant environments without needing to replicate the human body.
Physical AI systems can perceive environments, understand spatial context, make operational decisions, and act autonomously in real time across industrial and other settings. Physical AI systems move beyond static automation toward adaptive operations that continuously improve through interaction with the real world.
As with most tech trends, physical AI is driven by a coalescence of several technologies that have matured simultaneously. These include: multimodal sensing , edge computing, simulation environments, robotics foundation models, and world modeling systems. These technologies allow machines to collect information from the physical environment, interpret it in context, simulate outcomes before acting, and continuously refine performance through operational feedback loops.
